answer.label: Not Charles Bukowski — a paraphrase of Bertrand Russell
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording appears in none of Charles Bukowski’s books or interviews. It is a modern, smoothed-over paraphrase of a line Bertrand Russell wrote in his 1933 essay “The Triumph of Stupidity”: “the stupid are cocksure, while the intelligent are full of doubt.” Quote Investigator groups the sentiment across Yeats, Russell and Bukowski, but no source pins this precise sentence to Bukowski.

source.heading: The documented antecedent

docMeta.dd: Anonymous later paraphrase, mis-credited to Bukowski

source.excerpt: The fundamental cause of the trouble is that in the modern world the stupid are cocksure while the intelligent are full of doubt.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the idea across three figures: Yeats’s 1920 “The Second Coming” (“The best lack all conviction, while the worst / Are full of passionate intensity”), Russell’s 1933 essay, and a 1989 Bukowski interview line about writers — none of which is the popular sentence.
Russell’s exact 1933 wording — “the stupid are cocksure while the intelligent are full of doubt” — is preserved in his collected American essays and reproduced online.
On the Bukowski Forum, longtime scholars concluded the phrase “full of doubt” appears in none of his books and traced it back to Russell — a case of a paraphrase “wrongly attributed” to Bukowski.
source.excerptNote: Russell’s actual 1933 sentence — the “Bukowski” version is a rewrite of this line.

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording is an anonymous paraphrase with no identifiable published source, so no rights status can be asserted for it. The documented antecedent — Russell’s 1933 essay “The Triumph of Stupidity” — was first published in 1933 and would itself be handled as in-copyright (Bertrand Russell estate / The Bertrand Russell Peace Foundation).

author.name: Bertrand Russell
author.heading: About Bertrand Russell
author.bio: Bertrand Russell was a British philosopher, logician and social critic who won the 1950 Nobel Prize in Literature. His 1933 essay “The Triumph of Stupidity,” written as the Nazi movement rose in Germany, contains the line that the modern paraphrase reworks: “the stupid are cocksure, while the intelligent are full of doubt.” The polished “doubts…confidence” version that circulates today — often under Charles Bukowski’s name — is not Russell’s exact phrasing either.

misattribution.heading: Why Bukowski gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s most durable misattributions: a Bertrand Russell idea, smoothed into a punchier sentence and pinned on Charles Bukowski, whose blunt persona makes the line feel plausibly his.

items.why: The exact sentence appears in none of Bukowski’s books, and Bukowski scholars judge it not to be from his interviews either — the Bukowski Forum traced it to Russell. Bukowski’s own nearest remark (a 1989 Arete interview) was narrowly about writers: bad writers have self-confidence while good ones have self-doubt.
Russell’s 1933 essay “The Triumph of Stupidity” supplies the documented line the paraphrase rewrites, per Quote Investigator.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Bertrand Russell’s (1933); the exact “doubts…confidence” wording is an anonymous later paraphrase, and it is not Charles Bukowski’s — see Quote Investigator.

context.heading: A saying with three fathers
lead: The sentiment — that certainty runs inverse to intelligence — has been voiced independently by several writers, which is exactly why it drifts so easily from one famous name to another. Quote Investigator lines up W. B. Yeats’s 1920 “The Second Coming” (“The best lack all conviction, while the worst / Are full of passionate intensity”), Bertrand Russell’s 1933 essay, and a 1989 Bukowski interview as three distinct expressions of the same idea.

The version that went viral — “the intelligent people are full of doubts, while the stupid ones are full of confidence” — is closest to Russell’s phrasing but matches none of the three verbatim. It is best understood as a crowd-polished paraphrase that later acquired a celebrity byline.
context.pull: The idea is Russell’s; the wording is the internet’s; the byline is wrong.
